item.description:
As I watch the credits roll on Silent Hill: Townfall, it's hard to believe this is the same series that had, until just a few years ago, been neglected into near-irrelevance. Like 2025's excellent Silent Hill f, Townfall is a fascinating thing; a game of bold creative swings that's part inversion, subversion, and evolution of the near-three-decade survival horror series, charting its own idiosyncratic path while still feeling entirely Silent Hill.
Silent Hill f played a bit of a long game, reimagining so much of what the series could be in its shift from North America to 1960s-era rural Japan, that it took a while for that Silent Hill spirit to emerge from it all. Townfall, by contrast, rattles through so many of the series' classic touchpoints so fast - behold a sad man with a clearly guilty conscience roaming the darkly shifting melancholy mists in search of a woman - I was worried we might be looking at the kind of Silent Hill 2 cover act that nearly killed the series dead first time around. But instead, Townfall is far more ambitious than its early moments might suggest.
Geographically, of course, this is yet another kind of Silent Hill. Scottish indie developer Screen Burn, which created the acclaimed Observation and Stories Untold, shifts the fog again: this time to 1996 and St. Amelia; a small Scottish town on a remote island in the North Sea. And it's an exquisitely realised space, sharing the kind of slavish verisimilitude that made The Chinese Room's Everybody's Gone to the Rapture (a game Townfall shares a certain ambient kinship with) such a deeply transporting creation.
From the moment our confused protagonist Simon Ordell hefts himself out of the water beneath bleak Scottish skies - IV bag mysteriously taped to his shoulder, drip tube snaking into his hand - you can practically taste the sea salt in the air and feel the chill damp seeping into your bones. St. Amelia is a world of such convincing detail - the very British street signs, the blinking crossing lights, the cheery bunting, the local noticeboard ads - that it's engulfing even before you've stepped away from its weather-battered seafront into its cobbled market square.
Here, quaintly decorated shops - the local post office, a newsagent, a video store - jostle cosily along narrow streets, and it'd all look wonderfully picturesque if it wasn't for the rows of 'for sale' signs and 'closed for business' notices suggesting the decay had started even before the fog set in. And slowly, the world expands outward - toward pebbledashed terraced houses and blocks of flats, toward tatty pubs with gloomy beer gardens, and roadside cafes. Later, modernity encroaches with a shift to stark 70s brutalism, and as trite as it might be to say, St. Amelia really is as much a character as anything else in Townfall.
It's fascinating, too, watching Screen Burn reinterpret Silent Hill's iconography through a different cultural lens: gleaming white hospitals become cramped NHS wards, spacious malls now stark concrete shopping precincts. This world of fading industry and fractured community is a familiar one, albeit shattered - as we learn early on - by awful tragedy. Townfall's horrors aren't solely phantasmagorical, and Screen Burn infuses its tale with a quiet sort of rage as it grapples with themes of corporate colonisation and worker exploitation (here, the nurse isn't a shambling cleavage monster but a traumatised key worker reeling from the horrific death toll). It's social realism as a grounding force for the horror, and a powerful emotional throughline.
As for Simon, I suspect most people will clock his role in all of this even before the prologue is over. Which is fine. This isn't a game whose story - told with surprising directness for a series that traditionally delights in obfuscation - is particularly concerned with big twists. Rather it invokes Silent Hill's established narrative systems to explore ideas of interconnected grief and guilt (and there are some intriguing implications here for lore fans too).
Which probably all sounds very lofty. But Screen Burn, once Townfall's patient first chapter is over, absolutely does not skimp on the suffocating horror. That starts with its shift to first-person (technically Silent Hill 4 got there first, but only in its hubworld). It's a more limiting, vulnerable perspective compared to the series' usual third-person camera, and, combined with a focus on slow-paced, violence-avoidant stealth, makes for sometimes unbearable tension.
Combat isn't absent in Townfall but it's limited, mostly consisting of clumsy blocks and wild melee swings. And creatures - tumorous things with axe-like heads or grasping syringes that burst from puckered wounds - hit hard and pursue aggressively, making direct confrontation risky too. Even when a revolver is added to your arsenal later on, providing significantly more stopping power than the deteriorating wooden planks you'll be brandishing most of the time, it's got the kind of reload speed you could boil an egg by. It'll also draw the attention of every creature in a wide radius - and fights against multiple enemies rarely end well. So while brute force is possible, survival undoubtedly favours those with low squats and soft footfalls.
Enter your CRTV. Part Game Boy, part tiny portable television, it's a neat twist on Silent Hill's classic radio static early warning system. Move into an enemy infested area and you'll be greeted by a quick hiss of static, signifying that new signals have been added to its dial. Each represents a single patrolling creature, and once you've locked onto their signal, their isolated silhouette appears in the screen's roiling red static, but with no other visual clues.
This creates an unusual dynamic where you're often aware of distant enemies and their movements well before you've any sense of the area they're patrolling, and the resulting rhythm reminded me a little of original Silent Hill designer Keiichiro Toyama's cult classic horror game Siren. In that game, you'd arrive at a new perimeter, then, by peeking through the eyes of the monsters in the area, slowly build a fragmentary picture of the gauntlet to come. Townfall isn't quite the same, but the end result is similarly stressful in its deliberate withholding, forcing you to push forward with only a tentative grasp of the layout ahead and a rudimentary best-guess plan. You're not totally helpless, though: aside from that last-gasp revolver, you can arm yourself with rocks and bottles to stun enemies or draw them away from their patrols. And, alongside your supply of healing items, Simon's IV drip, if filled, can buy you a useful revive.
Simon, I should note, is a bit of an odd protagonist; something of a cipher in his own story, which makes him slightly dull company early on. But Townfall is a game about shifting perspective in other ways too. What, it seems to ask, about those other faces in the fog; those unwitting players in the protagonist's story? I've ummed and ahhed over how much to reveal here, but given the shift happens early, I'll just say this: Simon isn't the only playable character in Townfall. This allows for added narrative richness as events unfold through different eyes, but it also creates a natural way for Screen Burn to build tension by subverting its own rules.
Whenever Simon isn't in the picture, for instance, neither is the CRTV. Suddenly, your safety net is gone, forcing a more intimate form of stealth that pushes you deeper, more precariously, into enemy territory and increases your reliance on environmental cues: peeking around corners, listening for sounds, or watching for flickering streetlights as a creature passes below. Townfall's often expansive maps require constant adaptation too, as criss-crossing objectives pull you from claustrophobic corners to exposed spaces and back again. And invariably, just as you're settling into this newer rhythm, it's all-change once more.
There's a long sequence as Townfall enters its latter stretch that makes the Silent Hill 2 remake's prison level feel like a breezy afternoon stroll as it smothers the world in corpses, setting a grim game of spot-the-difference in motion as it gleefully, repeatedly sends you back and forth across this awful, twitching minefield. It's unrelentingly intense - almost unbearably so - but then Townfall reinvents itself again; teasing a sudden shift into power fantasy then immediately dashing hopes in a prolonged sequence of jumpscare hide-and-seek in near darkness.
Each new chapter brings its own ambient flavour too. At one point, daylight suddenly turns to night like a flicked lightswitch, yellow streetlamps giving the fog a queasy glow. The rust of Silent Hill's hellish otherworld is reimagined as a maze of stark concrete, artfully lit in shades of transfusion red and ambulance blue. Sometimes St. Amelia's skies turn crimson, recasting the town in striking silhouette as impossibly vast tangles of industrial pipes rend the once-familiar world. And while composer Akira Yamaoka's soundscapes are as much a part of the series' distinctive ambience as its suffocating fog, Townfall sees composer Anthony Scott Burns make a stellar series debut; capturing the texture of Yamaoka's music - the melancholy synths, the industrial cacophony - but with a beauty and violence of its own.
If Townfall stumbles, it's in its broader rhythms. Silent Hill's classic fogworld-otherworld shifts aren't just an aesthetic device, they're a vital pressure valve too, deflating high-anxiety states with quieter restorative lulls. But once its melancholy opening act is over, Townfall roars into high gear and pretty much stays there. Screen Burn clearly isn't oblivious to horror's critical ebb and flow, and it breaks up the stealth with some grimly inventive puzzles (one clever bit has faint echoes of the text-adventure-inspired Stories Untold, another sees a house shifting back and forth in time, which the studio uses - as it so often does - as an opportunity for subtle environmental storytelling). But Townfall's refusal to settle for long means that respite is brief, as you're invariably dragged through more enemy encounters on the way to a solution.
It is, perhaps, just a little too relentless, too keen to keep players held in wearying states of prolonged emotional extremes across its 15-or-so hour runtime. And without a true release, the tension steadily deflates; the already slightly too lengthy chapters increasingly outstaying their welcome. That's particularly true of a slightly fumbled closing chapter, set in easily the game's most blandly realised location. It unfortunately compounds some of Townfall's more irritating ticks - excessive backtracking through fussy enemy encounters, occasionally abstruse puzzle design - making them harder to overlook. And it drags it all out interminably at a point the story needs momentum. Thankfully, Townfall finds its footing again in time for the resolution, with a denouement (one of five possible endings) that's at once fitting for this idiosyncratic tale and very Silent Hill - even if it does feel like Screen Burn has, by then, made its point and then some.
Silent Hill: Townfall is, though, an often phenomenal ride; reverent to its roots, rich with ideas, and yes, properly unnerving too. And there is, I think, some pleasing symmetry in the fact the two grandaddies of the survival horror genre - Resident Evil and Silent Hill - have bookended the year with their own distinctive highs; one with a warm eye to the past, the other taking bolder, more experimental strides. Silent Hill has, from near-death, blossomed into something unexpected. Under the watch of Konami - itself undergoing a bit of a revival - and in the hands of talented studios with their own distinct sensibilities, it's transformed into one of gaming's most fascinating series. And long may its big creative swings continue.
A copy of Silent Hill: Townfall was provided for this review by Konami.

item.title: Activision has published a breakdown of the numbers behind cheating in its games, claiming cheating is big business, generating about £6.3 billion - $8.5bn - every year in account sales, boosting, and spoofing services. Read more
item.description:
Activision has published a breakdown of the numbers behind cheating in its games, claiming cheating is big business, generating about £6.3 billion - $8.5bn - every year in account sales, boosting, and spoofing services.
In a blog posted on the publisher's website, the publisher's cheat squad, Team Ricochet, said cheat subscriptions across 15 games alone generate around £2.6 billion ($3.5 billion).
RICOCHET Anti-Cheat doesn't end when your match does.Cheat makers operate around the world. So do we. We’re taking the fight directly to cheat sellers.Last weekend during the Closed Beta, we went to Ohio to takedown Elocarry.That’s not an isolated case... pic.twitter.com/IP69qlGgDD
Activision said it has "paired technical detection with sustained legal action to destabilise the cheat ecosystem at every level", disrupting more than 375 reseller operations, issuing more than 80 cease-and-desist demands, and shutting down 31 primary cheat vendors.
The publisher also claims cheat sellers regularly hide the fact their products have been detected, instead blaming outages on excuses like illness, surgery or car accidents to keep customers on side before admitting their cheats are no longer working.
Activision says the crackdown is also driving up costs for cheaters themselves, with subscriptions costing upwards of £75 ($100), spoofing tools adding further recurring fees, and some players spending more than £750 ($1,000) a year in total.
"Ultimately, cheating is a losing investment," the blog concluded. "Every time we identify and remove a bad actor, the money they spent cheating goes with them - all for a temporary ego boost. Ricochet Anti-Cheat keeps making cheating harder, riskier, and more expensive to sustain. Our layered systems add friction across the market, and that pressure changes behaviour.
"The ecosystem keeps changing. So do we."
Last month, Activision posted footage of one of its legal representatives turning up at the Ohio home of a notorious Call of Duty cheat seller and handing over a cease-and-desist order.
Modern Warfare 4 is set for release on 23rd October on PC, PS5, Xbox Series X/S and Switch 2. Activision is trying to convince players to pre-order the military shooter via $5 in store credit.

item.description:
Last week, we learned that Sony "stepped away" from Kojima Production's previously PlayStation-exclusive "action espionage" game Physint. Following the announcement, which saw Xbox take over publishing duties for the in-development title, a new report has claimed Sony's decision was the result of concerns over "budget, potential profitability and exclusivity".
Now, IGN has conducted an interview with Kojima that sheds a little more light on the situation. In the chat - which covers a range of topics including Kojima's fears for the future of the studio, the perils of working on multiple projects at once, and the implications of losing Sony resources - Kojima detailed how the conversation with the platform holder went, noting how that he was in a state of shock at the time, and finds the meeting difficult to recall.
"I don't remember so much of that meeting, to be honest with you," Kojima told IGN. "And my colleagues probably don't remember as well, so I can't really answer if you ask me what exactly they said. But, from my side, I love Sony. And I don't have any bad feelings against them because I know that it's a tough time in the game industry.
"Nothing could've prepared me for their decision to step away from the project. So I thought, "What am I going to do from tomorrow?" But from my side, I love Sony. And I don't have any bad feelings against them because I know that it's a tough time in the game industry."
Kojima noted that, during the call, Sony told him it could no longer fund development for the game, and that despite his awareness of the studio closures and job losses plaguing the games industry at the moment, he thought "Physint was OK, that Physint was safe".
Kojima then recalled his working relationship with Sony: "I've been working with them for like 30 years... Mr. Ken Kutaragi, Mr. Hirai - I was close with them. But it's not like that recently. I realised that, okay, this is the reality that they're giving me. It's the 10th anniversary of my studio. My studio might collapse, right?"
Later on in the article, Kojima Prodcutions issues a statement - not tied to Kojima personally - replying to accusations made in the Bloomberg article:
"None of the claims written came from any official or on-the-record source and as such we encourage you to take them with a dose of scepticism. Make no mistake, this was a serious situation for the studio with a range of potentially significant implications. While we recognise that the article may have caused alarm, we want to reassure you all, for the record: that the studio is in a healthy, profitable state, development for Physint continues to move forward with Xbox, and our relationship with PlayStation remains strong."
It seems Xbox, at least, is happy continue betting on Kojima and Kojima Productions - especially after making Physint and OD the headliners of its TGS show, earlier this week. "Betting on Kojima-san is an easy call. We believe in his team's ability to build triple-A games with groundbreaking, new IP and we believe in OD, Physint, and our growing partnership," an Xbox spokesperson said.

item.title: World of Warcraft: Forever, Blizzard's vanilla-flavoured spin-off built by the WoW Classic team, has already pulled in far more players than the studio expected. Read more
item.description:
World of Warcraft: Forever, Blizzard's vanilla-flavoured spin-off built by the WoW Classic team, has already pulled in far more players than the studio expected.
While the game isn't set to go live until 4th November and the rush of players to this week's beta caused disconnects and heavy lag, the team are nonetheless excited by the response to the upcoming launch.
As WoW Classic developer Josh Greenfield shared on Twitter/X: "Man, it was hard to sleep last night, I was so excited. Beta has been... crazy. The craziest numbers I've seen in 17 years working at Blizzard and almost eight years on classic."
He added: "We've got something really special here".
Man, it was hard to sleep last night, I was so excited. Beta has been... crazy. The craziest numbers I've seen in 17 years working at Blizzard and almost 8 years on classic.We've got something really special here.
World of Warcraft senior game producer Tom Ellis also took to Twitter/X detail why the test had struggled to meet demand.
"AHMAGERD, this game is 20 years old, how do you still suck at this!?!" he wrote.
Alright, now the dust has settled and you're just happily playing away, let's answer the most common question I've seen.1. AHMAGERD, this game is 20 years old, how do you still suck at this!?!a. Heh, fair enough, sort answer is, this is our BETA PTR environment stack, it's not…
"Heh, fair enough, short answer is, this is our BETA PTR environment stack, it's not a Production stack by a long, long, long, long, long, long shot. Betas for WoW aren't usually huge meter movers so this environment just isn't that powerful. This led to the first problem you saw today," he wrote.
"Shortly after we went live and when you got through the login queue (which is just http://B.Net protecting itself, rate limiting logins, normal!), you were disconnected. Ah. That's not quite right. This one took the longest of the issue today to figure out (and even then, was around half an hour I think?)," he added. "Our little BETA environment only uses one REGIONAL realm. Hrm, we should do a panel on WoW infra one day so any of this makes sense. Anyway...
By the end of the day, Blizzard had resolved the issues: "Marked live once again and you all poured in without fuss," Ellis said.

Blizzard finally officially confirmed World of Warcraft: Forever at last week's BlizzCon after
fans were obsessing over colours as dataminers pulled hues from Blizzard's website that were labelled under a curious "wow 2" tag, leading many to speculate that this referred to the rumoured World of Warcraft Camelot, or as it's better known, "Classic Plus", much like how Blizzard is now expanding Diablo 2.

item.title: The Last of Us director Bruce Straley has apologised to the God of War Laufey team at Sony Santa Monica for saying he was "not excited" about the upcoming game's gameplay. Read more
item.description:
The Last of Us director Bruce Straley has apologised to the God of War Laufey team at Sony Santa Monica for saying he was "not excited" about the upcoming game's gameplay.
Edge's latest cover story, entitled "The game industry is broken - can we fix it?", talked to nine industry figures, including Straley, about the industry's ongoing crisis of layoffs, ballooning budgets, and shrinking studios.
In the interview, Straley said he'll "probably never" make the triple-A game he actually wants to because modern blockbusters are "boring".
Straley - who spent 18 years at Naughty Dog, where he was game director on The Last of Us and co-director on the first two Uncharted games before leaving in 2017 - is working with a small team at Wildflower Interactive on Coven of the Chicken Foot.
"I have an idea for a triple-A game," he tells Edge. "I will probably never make it. I think the verbs and experiences we're delivering in the triple-A space are…I wanna say boring.
"God Of War Laufey, I look at that game, and every pixel is mindblowing," he added. "The amount of work and skill that's gone into every single frame… I've made those kinds of games, and I'm still blown away. But when I actually look at what you're doing in the game? I'm not excited.
I want to apologize to the Laufey team for dragging you all into this uninvited & unnecessary negative attention. I was trying to illustrate an industry concern & my mistake of naming your game is being used out of context & for clickbait. You don’t need this. I’m sorry. 🧵 pic.twitter.com/Ri2KgfJ4yY
"And that's nothing against the God Of War team. Just, across the board in triple-A, it feels like there's no opportunity to inject fresh, innovative ideas."
Writing on X/Twitter, he said: "I want to apologise to the Laufey team for dragging you all into this uninvited [and] unnecessary negative attention. I was trying to illustrate an industry concern [and] my mistake of naming your game is being used out of context [and] for clickbait. You don’t need this. I'm sorry.
"A journo asked me about the state of our industry. I mentioned a few concerns. One being the lack or [sic] innovation and risks taken in the AAA space. Tho[ugh] this isn't the team's fault!
"My fear is that our player base is getting tired of playing the same verbs for the last 20 years."
In a follow-up tweet Straley added: "My hypothesis: Our medium is unique because players are DOING a thing. There's a different physiological response than viewers who just WATCH a movie. This requires us creators to continue to push & create new experiences, or we run the risk of diminishing players' dopamine.
"Half-life 2 was released in 2004. Gears: 2006. Bioshock: 2007. Uncharted 2: 2009. The Last of Us: 2013. I feel like those games (and more) set the 'modern AAA' mold. Each felt like they were trying to create a new experience within AAA. But this is only one side of my concerns.
"ANYWAY... blah blah blah. I have thoughts about what's wrong and the possible serious harm done to our industry and how we might be able to fix it. But in trying to have a thoughtful conversation I stuck my foot in my mouth and mentioned Laufey, and that was my mistake."
Santa Monica Studio head of creative, Cory Barlog, recently confirmed that the next mainline, Kratos-starring God of War will pick up after the events of God of War Laufey.
God of War Laufey will release on 16th February 2027. It was revealed as one of the biggest in this year's Summer Game Fest season, and part of a record-breaking State of Play. The surprise reveal generated plenty of discussion, but most of the talk centred on the game's new protagonist, Faye.

item.description:
Nodusfall, aesthetically at least, is about as far from a typical HoYoverse game as you can get. Gone are the bright colours, cute creatures, and bountiful anime women. In their place, we get all the familiar trappings of dark fantasy: mysterious magics, vicious monsters, and a dingier kind of realism that - and I'm sure we've all thought it - feels a little bit Elden Ring. But from what I played at Gamescom, Nodusfall has the potential to shake off those FromSoftware comparisons and come into its own.
I'll admit to being a little worried at the beginning of my preview after learning it would consist of two boss battles fought in groups of four. After all, the majority of my co-op experience comes from RuneScape, a 25-year-old MMORPG primarily played with a mouse, and nobody wants to let their team down.
But first came the character selection. There were four options available in my demo: two focused around melee combat, two ranged. Both combat styles offered one character with healing-focused abilities which I immediately discounted - too much responsibility. The archer with a mechanical arm though? Inflicting heavy damage from a distance while taking care of any nasty surprises was definitely something I could do. Decision made, it was time to discover how my chosen role would actually play out in battle.
Nodusfall's combat, it turns out, is easy enough to get to grips with. There's your basic attack, which fills a gauge that eventually allows you to unleash a more powerful attack. Next, a secondary move. For my archer, this was a nifty - and enjoyable - bomb arrow which, once embedded in a foe's flesh, dealt extra when hit. Beyond that, each character has four unique abilities that operate based on cooldowns, some more generous than others.
My archer, for example, had an ability that essentially acted as a dodge - enabling her to jump backwards before firing off a powerful arrow - and another where she unleashed a spirit wolf. Since the wolf only deals damage in close quarters, I'd first have to dash towards a foe before using it, then follow it up with the dodge to regain some distance. All this, I should add, depletes stamina, but the bar is a generous one.
And I was thrilled to discover my archer had actual range. I could easily run around the edges of the battlefield, safe in the knowledge my attacks would still land - useful for self-preservation and for helping my fellow teammates out. If a teammate was in need of additional firepower or revival, I could easily weave myself back into the midst of battle. And in this way, it wasn't long before I found myself settling into Nodusfall's surprisingly satisfying fighting rhythm.
As for what you'll be fighting, Nodusfall's enemy design draws inspiration from different mythologies around the world. In the demo, for instance, I fought Qiongqi, a creature from Chinese mythology depicted here as a griffin-like beast, and the Maldrake, your more traditional dragon. And HoYoverse has crafted some truly impressive monster encounters that I found myself wanting to stop and properly appreciate - which is pretty hard when the object of your appreciation is also trying to bite your head off.
Each boss battle is structured the way you'd typically expect - multiple stages, each with a new health bar - but, out of the two, the Maldrake was by far my favourite. Since it's a dragon, it attacks by doing the typical dragon things: fire-breathing, jaw-snapping, wing-whacking. Yet, during the fight's opening stage, I noticed something a little bit odd: human-like arms protruding from its chest. The secret behind these arms reveals itself about midway through the battle, when a knight rips itself out of the Maldrake's torso, killing it in the process. Thus the Maldrake fight becomes the Maldrake Knight fight.
Compared to the fairly slow and predictable dragon, the Maldrake Knight is a dangerously fast sword and polearm wielder who you don't want to get cornered by. It can also unleash puddles of black goo, which sap your health if stepped in. All of the strategies I'd been developing for the dragon had to be immediately thrown aside in order to adapt to this very different enemy who just loved tossing people in the air. And I hope HoYoverse can bring the same fun unpredictability to other fights, creating a similar need for experimentation.
Of course, given Nodusfall is a free-to-play title from a studio best known for its gacha games, there are questions to be asked about how this will be monetised. The developer says characters will be unlockable via continuous play rather than the banner system other HoYoverse games like Genshin Impact employ, and so cosmetic monetisation is being considered. Beyond that, however, specifics are limited so we'll have to wait to learn more.
I didn't know what to expect going into Nodusfall's preview, but I had a surprisingly great time. Combat is fast-paced without ever becoming overwhelming, bosses are compelling, and co-op is engaging while remaining approachable. I am, though, curious to learn more about solo play. As to whether Nodusfall can carve out its own niche among the games it's clearly drawing inspiration from, that remains to be seen. From what I've played, though, it's looking promising and I'll be watching its progress during the coming year.
This preview is based on a preview at Gamescom in Cologne, Germany. HoYoverse provided flights and accommodation.

Anyway! What have you been playing this week?
Here's another question: do you remember what you were playing last week? You don't have to! The What We've Been Playing archive has you covered.
Let's get the obvious one out of the way first: I play this every day, still. My pack luck has been dreadful with the Team Rocket set - duplicates of shinies I have no interest in (Seaking, anyone?) but still missing genuinely useful cards from the main set such as Team Rocket's Raticate ex. Nightmare. Anyway, I've loved the Rocket set itself - it's offered a rare bit of playfulness, and the artworks have been wonderful on the cards, even if the meta's a little stale.
Yes I know I said the review would be ready soon, and I promise it is actually going to be ready very soon, but: it is not ready right now. I'm still thoroughly enjoying it but finding it slow going, and amid other games that have had deadlines come and go - see: ol' Wolverine - it's had to temporarily go on the back burner. Shout out to the Anakin level though. And hopefully slightly more sophisticated thoughts than this from me are coming actually soon.
I'm a bit of a newcomer to D&D proper, having dabbled very briefly forever ago but never got going with a regular group. I'm now very much in one, and it's a treat - although progress through the actual "main quest" of our "campaign" is remarkably slow (I gather that's kind of standard).
My character is a Loxodon - think a Kajiit but an elephant-person instead of cat-person - with a background as a kind of wandering cleric. The rest of the party is, frankly, absolutely feral, and so I've been trying to balance that out with a character who wishes to be a bit more of a pacifist. There's also a deeply suspicious Tiefling warlock on our crew, who I've been tasked with keeping an eye on by the DM. It's made me into a kind of cross: part weary Gandalf trying to wrangle stray Hobbits, part chin-stroking Brother William of Baskerville. Most of the time it's a case of my friends trying to hit things they shouldn't, and me subsequently putting them to sleep until they calm down. (And that's very fun).
Bonus freelancer pick here (or ominous freelance hijacking, if you're feeling naughty). The first Moonlighter game - the one where you sell dusty relics in a shop, then moonlight as a sword-swinging dungeon explorer in search of even more sellable relics - never quite grabbed me as much as I thought it should. This new sequel? I've already sunk way too much time into the moreish roguelike since its early access exit.
The difference here, I think, is that there's always a meaningful new upgrade or shiny weapon or potion enhancement or shop decoration or blobby wobbly pet to save money for. And each one of them can quite drastically change how you approach your next procgen run or shift on the shop floor. It's a really satisfying ride to get stuck on, and the much improved monster bashing doesn't hurt.

item.title: Former PlayStation executives Shuhei Yoshida and Adam Boyes have recreated their iconic "this is how you share your games on PS4" moment - now with a very timely game-less picture. Read more
item.description:
Former PlayStation executives Shuhei Yoshida and Adam Boyes have recreated their iconic "this is how you share your games on PS4" moment - now with a very timely game-less picture.
No matter which side of the console war you sat on in 2013, there's a good chance Sony's 'Used Game Instructional Video' reached you. In the months leading up to the launch of the PS4 and Xbox One, Microsoft's restrictive game-sharing plans became hugely controversial and Sony decided to take advantage of the negative fan frenzy with one short clip.
PlayStation's president of first-party studios, Shuhei Yoshida, and head of third-party relations, Adam Boyes, stood in front of a camera and explained to folks how game-sharing worked on the company's then-next-gen console. Step one? Yoshida handed Boyes a physical copy of Killzone: Shadow Fall. Step two? There was none. That was all. The video racked up 21m views in the past 13 years and has since become one of the defining moments of the PS4's launch.
Now, Yoshida shared that he reunited with Boyes while at Tokyo Game Show 2026 in a new online post. "Met with a best friend," he wrote, alongside a picture of the duo recreating their famous game-sharing pose. Quite fittingly, neither have a physical game to share.
Met with a best friend :D @amboyes @PlayStation_jp #TGS2026 pic.twitter.com/2ZjsrLMNaP
Yoshida and Boyes weren't outright throwing shade at Sony's disc-less future, but fans obviously interpreted it as a mocking dig regardless. "This is how you share games with your friends in 2028," one reaction post tweeted.
Earlier this summer, Sony announced it would no longer manufacture discs for new PlayStation games starting in 2028. The company didn't wait for the body of physical gaming to go cold before it began repurposing its lone disc-making factory, either, leading to months of backlash from players who like to actually own the games they buy. Fans even tried to organise protests against PlayStation's all-digital future, though the console maker insisted it was sticking to its guns. Gaming analysts told Eurogamer the company's plans would be a "hammer blow" to traditional game stores and physical retailers.

item.title: Rockstar Games' latest leak seemingly includes a nearly 200GB version of GTA 5's source code, suggesting the developer started and then scrapped plans for a Liberty City DLC, alongside very early files related to GTA 6. Read more
item.description:
Rockstar Games' latest leak seemingly includes a nearly 200GB version of GTA 5's source code, suggesting the developer started and then scrapped plans for a Liberty City DLC, alongside very early files related to GTA 6.
The Grand Theft Auto and Red Dead Redemption maker has dealt with quite a lot of leakage these last few years, and new online reports now indicate the tap is still dripping. The leaks apparently total around 192GB of newly accessible files, reportedly revealing tons of stuff cut from GTA 5.
Fans have eagerly been combing through the data and it looks like they've unearthed everything from cut dialogue, scrapped missions, unused assets, a really rough version of GTA 6's map and ambitious GTA 5 DLC plans that never crossed the finish line, including several files reportedly related to Liberty City. YouTuber TJGM even posted an outline of the supposed Liberty City DLC map's shoreline, showing off a much larger playable space than GTA 4's take on New York City.
"This isn't a screenshot included in the leak," they tweeted after. "This is data viewed in CodeWalker and then screenshotted after. It also includes many other Rockstar tools, source code and other things that are legit and easily verifiable."
There's also some online speculation suggesting the Liberty City DLC might have been put on ice for Rockstar Games to use later down the line in a potential GTA 6 expansion, though I haven't found any evidence of that so far.
With the iconic locale back in the limelight, fans have been pointing to a screenshot of Liberty City in GTA 5's engine that was purportedly found on a Rockstar artist's portfolio a decade ago as proof the expansion was somewhat far in development before being canned.
In the years since its release, we've heard quite a lot about the other GTA 5 DLCs that never came to be. Trevor Philips actor Steven Ogg previously spilled info about a "James Bond Trevor" DLC that would've had the wildcard character working undercover for the government. Rockstar apparently "shot some stuff" for the side story, before the studio put all its eggs into the GTA Online basket. Some Agent Trevor materials are also reportedly part of this newest leak, though it's not yet clear to what extent.
A former senior camera artist and digital cinematographer at the studio, Joseph Rubino, also spoke on the Agent Trevor DLC a couple of years ago. "We split our teams into two, so I stayed on GTA Online and then this DLC, which Steven Ogg was a very important part of, and then some of the team overlapped and went to [Red Dead Redemption 2] early on," he said. "When GTA Online came out, it was so much of a cash cow and people were loving it so much that it was hard to make an argument that a standalone DLC would out-compete that… Looking back now I would say that you could probably do both, but that was a business decision that they made and I was a little upset about that."

item.title: Marvel's Wolverine has been in the hot seat over the last week or so, but mixed reviews and internet memes seemingly haven't put a dent in the superhero game's adamantium frame. item.description:
Marvel's Wolverine has been in the hot seat over the last week or so, but mixed reviews and internet memes seemingly haven't put a dent in the superhero game's adamantium frame. A new report states the latest from Insomniac Games has already sold almost 2m copies, with more than a fifth coming from physical sales.
Alinea Analytics' Rhys Elliott today reported that Marvel's Wolverine has moved around 1.9m copies in its first three days and, thus, dropped a fat bag of cash into PlayStation's lap. The figure apparently includes a million copies that came from pre-launch digital pre-orders. Altogether, the divisive action game's made upwards of $130m so far.
While Sony itself plans on ending production of discs for new PlayStation games in 2028, there seems to be plenty of demand for physical versions of its new blockbuster. According to the report, 22.9% of revenue came from physical editions.
Interestingly, Marvel's Wolverine's physical-to-digital ratio is slightly heavier on the digital side than some of the PS5's other big hitters. A previous Alinea Analytics report claimed Insomniac Games' last superpowered romp, Marvel's Spider-Man 2, made 35% of its PS5 revenue from physical sales. Around 46% of Astro Bot's sales also came from disc-based copies, while Ghost of Yotei's physical split was 37.6%.
Keep in mind, Marvel's Wolverine hasn't been on store shelves for very long at all and the holiday season could well make a difference in that percentage split over the coming weeks and months.
Regardless, Logan's early success already has him leaping, claws out, over almost every other PlayStation Studios game this year, too - Marvel's Wolverine's impressive 1.9m haul puts it above Saros, Marathon and Marvel Tokon. The vast majority of people who bit the bullet for Logan previously played Marvel's Spider-Man (82%) and Spider-Man 2 (70%), as well. There's also quite a bit of interesting overlap between Marvel Rivals players and Wolverine's new standalone adventure - 43% of players have touched the hit hero shooter.
It's still early days for Marvel's Wolverine, of course, but it looks like the divisive conversation around the game hasn't hurt sales all too much. Take a look at any number of gaming-centric online forums and you'll most likely find a couple threads mocking the game's persistent 'fart scent' trail or hand-holdy design. Eurogamer's Wolverine review called it "just fine."

item.description:
We're still about six months out from the release of Final Fantasy 7 Revelation, the final part of the FF7 Remake trilogy. But, already, there is a lot of discussion about the size of the game; whether it's all the divisive side activities on offer in the title, or the fact it won't be shipping totally on-disc at launch thanks to the amount of stuff it'll feature, director Naoki Hamaguchi is already fielding a lot of questions about 'size versus quality' in the last game in the Remake series.
In a new interview with VGC, the outspoken director notes that he's "not worried about the scale". He goes on to explain that the reason the game can't ship on disc (or even two discs, like Rebirth did) is because he's expecting the file size to be absolutely massive.
"Things are still getting worked out, but it’s probably going to be around 200GB of game," he says to VGC. "I understand there are a lot of opinions about this topic, but at the end of the day, the fact is we need to overcome the hardware to a certain extent."
Rebirth weighs in at 91GB on Switch 2, 145GB on PS5, 169GB on Xbox Series, and 155GB on PC, so depending on format, Revelation looks set to be up to twice as large as the last game in the series. Woof. The game will also receive two bonus DLC packages post-launch, and these will be similar in size to Remake's Intermission DLC, per Hamaguchi. "It's best to imagine the DLC like what we did with Intermission: digging deeper into the characters of Vincent and Sephiroth. In regard to whether those stories take place in the past or the present, I’m not going to tell you that now, but we’re excited to reveal that."
As the sort of sicko that routinely goes over 100 hours for my RPG reviews, I must say this both excites and terrifies me. For consumers, I have seen a lot of discussion this week about game length, thanks to the previously-linked Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave review - it seems, understandably, that games with a runtime of over 100 hours are simply too demanding for many adults with lives, jobs, and responsibilities to consider.
Final Fantasy 7 Revelation launches 8th April, 2027 for Xbox Series X/S, PlayStation 5, PC, and Nintendo Switch 2, and I'm curious to see if the trilogy will be able to stick the landing, or whether the whole thing will crumble under the weight of all this open world ambition. I've spoken to Hamaguchi about this before, and his answers to my concerns about open world game design put my mind at ease, at least.

item.description:
The first time I ate mold was like something out of a Victorian morality play. It was in boarding school, when fuzzy blue-grey discs would sometimes appear on the bottom of a quiche, or after I saw one of the kitchen ladies use a cleaning rag to cover a tray of cauliflower cheese. We were told it was a good source of protein, and because I complained, I had to collect rubbish for a weekend in my school uniform. Outside the realm of edible mushrooms and respectable fungi and polite society, the idea of eating mold is kinda gross. But here I am, in Control Resonant, faced with the Temptation of Saint Mycology, while my handler screams in my ear for me to put the mold down. I will not. I'm Dylan Faden, and this is Jackass.
Dylan, who became an indentured lab rat at age ten, never got to watch Jackass, because up until five minutes ago he was in a coma, and before that, he was possessed by a malevolent entity called the Hiss. His AWOL sister Jesse, the Director of the Federal Bureau of Control, oversaw a seven-year lockdown to contain the Hiss in the Oldest House after the events of the first game; in the present, the Hiss escapes into Manhattan and everything hits the proverbial fan. Dylan must help the Bureau deal with a new threat as the city is cut off from the outside world, while also searching for Jesse, who may not even be on the same dimensional plane.
I loved Control. I have fond memories of exploring New York and learning how bad the city smells after a spring rain. I love over-the-top paratextual worldbuilding and the X-Files and goofy nods to new weird literary themes. The best part of Control was how well it mythologised a vast and indifferent bureaucracy, thanks largely to the SCP Foundation, a collaborative online fiction project that Remedy drew on for inspiration, and how that arcane mythology imprinted so perfectly on a whole administration of dyed-in-the-wool civil servants and 1960s-era pneumatic tubes. Hell hath no petty like a disgruntled worker filing HR complaints while a hivemind takes over the building, and together, all of the game's documents and recordings and found items told a banger piece of speculative fiction that vibrated on the same dysfunctional frequency as the House. The tonal contrast of bland mundanity and eldritch freakshow isn't a new combo, but it works really well for a reason, and it was a huge part of what gave Control the juice.
Remedy has since described each Control game as a reflection of each respective Faden protagonist. Unfortunately this makes Control the tighter and more narratively cohesive sibling, while Control Resonant is kind of all over the place. Big sister was a game that understood the genres it drew from, and most importantly, knew what it wasn't (the combat systems weren't very good then, and they're still not great now, but let's be real – no one is playing Remedy games for the combat). Little brother, though, feels pulled in different directions, and follows a more emotional path as it gets deeper into family dynamics, few of which are particularly striking, and, with a couple of exceptions, don't add much to the story that 1) you can't infer yourself and 2) wouldn't be better off left in the periphery of the player's imagination.
Control Resonant is by necessity a different creature from Control. For starters, it's much more of a triple-A-flavoured action RPG, with a big wide map of tiny little markers for everything from persons of interest and repeating world events. There's a discernible loss of focus now that we're outside the Oldest House, whose shifting architecture was a core part of how Control cultivated and maintained such an effective atmosphere. The Oldest House was a moody, ancient Brutalist cocoon full of secrets – you couldn't trust the walls around you, which was a neat setting for getting sucked into the bowels of a government agency. Dylan is a maladapted sadboy experiencing the real world for the first time as an adult, and to this end, a big overwhelming city makes sense to tell this type of story. Manhattan fragmented and literally turned upside-down because of reality-changing interdimensional physics – there is at least one Inception joke in the game – feels appropriate for a guy who just came out of a coma, but it also means all that smartly-styled weirdness gets diluted into Marvel-style blockbuster flatness. There's just about no suspense left when you can climb onto a rooftop, look out, and see all the areas brewing with Hiss or Mold.
Accordingly, the open-ended world (Remedy is keen to remind us this is, technically, not an open world) lends itself much more to an FBC team-building group-effort situation – Dylan's handler, agent Zoe de Vera, plays the straight man buffer between Dylan and the bureau and tries to make peace with her own role in an organisation that made his life hell. World events involve supporting FBC rangers in the field (defend the cargo, protect the worker, and so on) and after a certain point Dylan unlocks a chore board for garden-variety escort missions and fetch quests. He meets different factions within the bureau (shoutout to the mold people and Langston) as he tries to prove that he isn't a homicidal meat puppet anymore. There's the usual triple-A dance between big save-the-world story beats and minor side stories where all the best writing is hidden, but at times, like when Zoe radios Dylan to do nothingburger tasks after a big urgent plot reveal, the pacing suffers. The cumulative effect is a kind of narrative sprawl, an inversion of the purpose that shaped Jesse's journey in Control. I should know something about how turgid and dull main questlines are: I play Final Fantasy 14.
Combat-wise, Dylan is a melee guy. His main abilities are straightforward button-spammers with a sprinkling of tactical support skills; new combat abilities are learned by defeating bosses called Resonants. His weapon is the Aberrant, essentially a paranatural metal bar that can morph into whatever the moment needs (it also houses a familiar friend from the first game). In line with Remedy's action-RPG aspirations, they've refined skill trees to hew closer to familiar class conventions, so players can choose a high-crit build or focus on crowd control and AOE attacks. I use Glaive as my primary ability – it gives the Aberrant a big swing with a knockback – and start golfing my way through mobs. It does not feel as meaty as I would like it to, and this is certainly not Dynasty Warriors, but I eventually find joy in a secondary fire punch skill that is exceptionally powerful against Mold. Inquiring minds will want to know if Control's combat has improved, and the unfortunate answer is not really.
Traversal abilities are learned from Faults, which are sort of interdimensional "thin" places where Dylan senses Jesse. Faults offer interactive storytime and explore the Fadens' link as siblings united by trauma, which in turn involves a lot of repetitive leaping and dashing paired with childhood dysfunction. Most of this is Mike Flanagan-level melodramatic, and I am not a fan of what Mike Flanagan has done to horror and the way it intersects so limply with therapy and trauma.
Because this is Remedy, the game hammers home its hyper-meta themes of refraction and recursion at every possible opportunity, so I am, to an extent, prepared to get lost and do things over and over again. But when the gravity mechanics kick in and Dylan has to move between planes on a timer, navigating becomes trickier and puzzles become a little more involved, and when you throw in a mess of dynamic markers and deliberately disorienting gameplay, some of which demand falling from a great height on a precise trajectory, hitting a nice flow can get frustrating (there were also a couple times when my Inception shenanigans got me stuck in a chasm behind a wall).
Is messing with gravity cool? Did you like Gravity Rush? Yes, walking up walls is always cool, but a lot of the "Dylan swooping around New York" stuff plays out like Spider-Man helping literal puppies and saving civilians. Frankly, I could do routine superheroing in a better action game – this is not why I want to play a Control game.
As a result, Control Resonant doesn't truly hit its stride until Dylan is beneath the Oldest House in the Underpass. Here, my second-favorite story arc unfolds through reports and recordings – an understated cosmic horror workplace drama podcast, set against a backdrop of monolithic office columns and minimalist Zdzisław Beksiński landscape vibes (there is also an Interstellar-inspired questline in the adjacent area, which feels like one too many Nolans for a single meal). Some of Resonant's best writing and voice performances live down here, and it snaps me back into the game.
Further in, there's a massively unexpected appearance of a whole other genre that will delight a lot of people (I was bewildered and appreciative), and I love it when the game goes hard into the special interest subjects and shows me intense pockets of drama happening in a forgotten corner of the subway. Dylan's thing is drawing, and there's an art-therapy-esque feature where he'll see something that reminds him of a memory that he can recreate with found objects and sketch; assembling these makeshift tableaus is silly and charming but I didn't take it seriously until the game wanted me to make a dragon out of rubbish and subway cones and I couldn't find the last piece. I want to finish that dragon, and it will haunt me until I do.
Remedy projects are visually and technically lovely to behold, and this one is no different. The game looks good, period. I love the FBC uniform design here, with the paper bag-like headwear that feels like a page from the Venture Bros henchman universe. I will eat up every second of Matthew Porretta's screentime as Casper Darling, and I love a good bit of stylised shadow puppetry. These are all load-bearing parts of the Control universe. But there's only so much you can do to spice up a repeated landscape of city blocks and same-y military blockades without losing aesthetic potency. Naturally there are big moments of spectacle – visual spectacle is likewise a pillar of the Control experience – but after a certain point it feels like Resonant leans a bit too much on quirky weirdness (weird dogs! floating vending machines! warring aliens!) in New York, as a stand-in for narrative quality and substance. Not much comes close to the "oh shit, cool" moments or impeccable vibes that made Control special.
I don't think anyone expects perfect coherence from an SCP-inspired setting, and honestly I don't think it matters that the game isn't entirely clear about its ending, either. But there's something missing. Perhaps it's the sense that the game tried to incorporate too much, and spread itself too wide. The contrast between Control's maximalist approach to paratextual storytelling and its minimalist design felt sharp and savvy. Resonant, though, feels like it's trying to have too many fingers in too many pies.
I realise that Remedy rebukes the idea of Control Resonant being an open-world game, and it's not quite as freewheeling and permissive as that, but Resonant feels like it's chasing the hallmarks of a live-service game while trying, only partly successfully, to echo the very deliberate structure and style of the genre storytelling that worked so well in the first game. You cannot make a good game whose whole cryptic conceit hinges on smart unconventional worldbuilding, and also shoehorn in the most deadening part of MMOs – world events, the equivalent of daily chores – without bringing the whole narrative party down. It's not a question of giving us something we haven't seen before. It's a question of being able to sustain that distinct, uncanny weirdness that brought Control to life. And to expand on that core magic, without muddying what made it special in the first place.
A copy of Control Resonant was provided for this review by Remedy Entertainment.

item.description:
Nintendo is having a pretty good time of it at the moment. Last year, we learned that the Switch 2 became the fastest selling video game hardware device in US history, usurping the PS4's golden record. Then, earlier this year, we learned that Switch 2 sales reached nearly 20m almost one year after release, making it the second-fastest selling console in US history. Buoyed by the runaway successes of games like Pokopia and other first-party hits, not even the reality of a hardware price rise seems to be hobbling Nintendo's momentum.
And it seems the company is keen to keep this pace up. "We're at the beginning of Nintendo Switch 2," says Nintendo of America COO, Devon Pritchard in an interview with Variety. "This is just beginning and we've already had some really wonderful experiences, both ours and third-party come to the table and I can't wait to see what the system is going to do and what our talented developers will bring to the table."
She goes on to point out that the publisher's success isn't just in hardware and software, but in Nintendo's recently acquired popularity at the box office, too. "We're working with Sony Pictures. We are going to have a movie come out in the end of April," she notes, referring to The Legend of Zelda. "We're very excited about that". No doubt; Nintendo and Illumination earned $1bn from The Super Mario Galaxy Movie at the last count, pulling in a third of that ($372.6m) in the opening weekend alone.
Whilst Pritchard is certainly excited about the games the company has on the docket - she namechecks The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, specifically - it seems her eyes are drawn more readily to the film partnerships. "But again, those partnerships and touchpoints with companies like Sony and Sony Pictures around how we can bring those experiences more broadly to not only our current players and fans but to new ones," she says, "I think that's one of the most exciting things for us over the next few years."
Safe to say, then, that Nintendo is putting a lot of effort into its expanding cinematic world. The last we heard about the next big project - The Legend of Zelda film which is just called "The Legend of Zelda", sans subtitle - was in a dedicated Zelda Direct at the beginning of September. We've not even seen a proper trailer yet, but we know that the initial shoot has wrapped filming in New Zealand (after starting the shoot in October 2025). So here's hoping we see some footage of the final product soon.
"There are more channels for content than ever before," Pritchard concludes when asked about how Nintendo plans to stand out in a media landscape more competitive than ever before. "Content is available 24/7. So I think you hear a lot of times, people saying, we are competing for consumers' time and I think what's unique is that Nintendo is focused instead on building experiences that create relationships that last generations. And I think that's a different kind of focus for us. But that really is where we put our time and our energy... how do we create those fun experiences? And that becomes the test: is something fun? It sounds simple, of course it's not."
Lets see if the company's belief in its product and audience lasts through the current industry woes; the combination of an industry crunch, rising hardware prices, and lower consumer spend is having a pretty disasterous effect elsewhere - but it seems Nintendo is so far weathering the storm.

item.title: Rockstar has remained very tight-lipped about GTA 6's multiplayer component, the potential successor to GTA 5's incredibly popular Grand Theft Auto Online, not yet commenting on whether it will even launch one. All we know currently is that when Grand Theft Auto 6 arrives on 19th November, it'll only include the single-player campaign. Read more
item.description:
But, in an interview with Bloomberg, Twitch CEO Dan Clancy has seemingly revealed GTA 6 multiplayer's launch window. "We spent a lot of time talking with Rockstar about their plans, and also helping them think about how they can engage our creators," he said. "You are going to see this big bump with GTA 6, but then an even bigger one next year when they launch multiplayer."
Here, it's worth noting that GTA 5's GTA Online mode arrived two weeks after the main game launched, but Red Dead Online - the multiplayer mode for Red Dead Redemption 2, and a more recent indicator of how Rockstar handles these staggered rollouts - went live seven months after launch.
The 'next year' referenced by Clancy here is, of course, wonderfully vague. It suggests we could see GTA Online Mk. II (that's a name I'm giving it, not anything official) launch as early as January, some two months after the big single-player release, or as far out as the end of 2027. What's more likely, though, is that we'll see a similar cadence to Red Dead Redemption 2, with GTA Online coming closer to summer than spring.
If you're worried about Rockstar dropping support for the current iteration of GTA Online, I wouldn't be too concerned. In 2025, Strauss Zelnick, boss of Rockstar parent company Take-Two, told IGN it's smart when it comes to legacy brands, and knows that people don't necessarily drop their old toys just because there are new ones on the shelves.
"I'm going to speak theoretically only because I'm not going to talk about a particular project when an announcement hasn't been made," Zelnick explained. "But generally speaking, we support our properties when the consumers are involved with those titles. As an example, we launched NBA 2K Online in China, I think originally in 2012 if I'm not mistaken. And then we launched NBA 2K Online 2 in China in 2017, if I'm not mistaken. We did not sunset Online 1. They both are still in the market and they serve consumers and they're alive and we have this massive audience."
"So we've shown a willingness to support legacy titles when a community wants to be engaged with them."
This latest news follows another flurry of GTA 6 announcements in the run-up to its November release. This week, we got word of the inevitable GTA 6 soundtrack, and last week saw all Grand Theft Auto 6's worldwide unlock times revealed ( Xbox owners can seemingly still use the old 'New Zealand trick' to play early, if they want to). Ahead of launch day, it's also worth remembering that multiple retailers have issued warnings that GTA 6 codes are region-locked, so make sure you're buying the right copy for the region you're in.
Amid the build-up to GTA 6's release, Rockstar Games and the Independent Workers Union of Great Britain (IWGB) are currently engaged in the final tribunal hearing relating to the sudden firing of 31 Rockstar North employees nearly a year ago, allegedly as part of a union-busting initiative by Rockstar.
